Manu
Tradition speaks of fourteen Manus who respectively formed the different Manvantaras. Of these, Svāyambhuva Manu is the author of Manusmṛti. See [Page-179a] Kane, HDS. I. i. p. 311.
According to tradition, the smṛti was passed on to Manu from Bhṛgu (Manusmṛti I. 60-61). Hence the text is ascribed to Bhṛgu in some catalogues.
For problems regarding the authorship of the smṛti, details about the a., an. the textual problems, see Kane, HDS. I. i. sn. 31.
(Svāyaṃbhuva). dh. writer. q. in Gautama D.. sūtra 21. 7; Āp. D.. sūtra 11. 6; 13. 11; often by Śaṅkara in his Br. sūtra bhāṣya IV. 2. I. 3; in Ācāramayūkha of Nīlakaṇṭha, VRI. IV. 10195. Extr. p. 495; Prāyaścittaviveka of Śūlapāṇi. VRI. IV. 10501; Śūdrakamalākara of Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa, son of Rāmakṛṣṇabhaṭṭa. VRI. V. 10296 (inc.). Extr. p.. 499-500.
For full account of Manu an. Manusmṛti, see Kane, HDS. I. i. Sn. 31; Śp. 75. 11; 39, 7; 37, 57; 75, 60; 75, 64; 91. 11; 91. 12.

Mantrakalpataru
by Puruṣottamadeva Mahārāja (1466-97 A. D.), son of Kapilendradeva, founder of the Gajapati dynasty of Orissa an. father of Gajapati Pratāpa-rudradeva. A big work comprising the Bhuvaneśvarīpallava in 18 stabakas. The introduction (6 ff. in Cuttack 112) describes the wars waged by Mahārāja Puruṣottama Deva in South India, in the 15th Cent. The author hails his victories a. favours of Goddess Bhuvaneśvarī, to whom a temple was dedicated by him a. Puri. An epitome of the essence of Sammohanatantra, Bhuvanādhipatantra, Sarvāgama-tantra, Prapañcasāra, Śaktisāra-samuccaya, Śāradātilaka, etc.
